title: NVIDIA Q1 FY2026 Earnings Call Transcript

sections.prepared_remarks: NVIDIA reporting Q1 FY2026 revenue $44.1 billion, up 262 percent year over year. Data Center $39.9 billion, up 427 percent. We are seeing broad-based acceleration across every customer set. Hyperscalers building AI supercomputers: Microsoft deploying 100,000+ Blackwell GPUs in Azure, Meta's Llama AI supercomputer. Sovereign AI: Japan, UAE, France all building national GPU infrastructure with NVIDIA. Enterprise AI: banks, hospitals, retailers deploying private AI on NVIDIA infrastructure. The shift to accelerated computing from general purpose computing is accelerating faster than most expected. Blackwell Ultra sampling Q4 2025, Rubin in 2026. Our total addressable market for data center compute and networking is $1 trillion over the next several years. We have significant supply commitments and continued inventory management discipline. Compute and networking demand exceeds supply. Customer demand is broad-based and long-cycle. We are expanding our supply chain with additional foundries, packaging partners, and memory suppliers. The NVIDIA AI ecosystem now has 6 million developers. CUDA downloads grew 3x year over year — the largest developer platform shift in history.
sections.financial_highlights: Revenue $44.1 billion, EPS $0.96, gross margin 78.4 percent — a company record driven by Blackwell unit economics. We expect Q2 revenue $50 billion. Gross margins in the high-70s. Data Center is now a $160 billion annualized revenue business. We've added three new hyperscalers — Oracle, CoreWeave, and Tesla — each deploying massive GPU clusters. Robotic simulation platform Omniverse has 120,000 enterprise customers. Automotive revenue hit a record $700 million in Q1. Gaming grew 18 percent to $3.7 billion. We invested $3.1 billion in R&D this quarter. Cash from operations $21.5 billion. We deployed $8.4 billion in buybacks. Our AI supply chain is resilient with 99 percent on-time delivery despite massive scale.
sections.qanda_session:
Stacy Rasgon: Jensen, your margin is at record levels and you guide to the mid-70s going forward. But you're also talking about massive capacity expansion. Where exactly do margins bottom, and do we think this is really the peak of the margin cycle? In other words, is this margin sustainable?

Jensen Huang: Stacy, our gross margins reflect the value our products deliver. Our customers achieve 5x to 15x improvement in AI training cost per token using NVIDIA versus any alternative. That's the pricing power of genuine technology leadership. Is 78 percent the peak? Maybe, maybe not. What's important is that as Blackwell Ultra and Rubin launch with higher ASP, they carry comparable or better margins. The software attach is growing — NIM microservices and CUDA platform generate revenue that didn't exist two years ago. As the installed base scales, the software revenue scales with it. We see enterprise software growing from a small base to a meaningful contributor within five years. All of this suggests a structurally higher margin floor. You're not buying a chip company — you're buying a platform company with software and services compounding.

Vivek Arya: Colette, on the demand picture — we hear conflicting signals about inference capex. Some hyperscalers are signaling they may moderate GPU purchases as training demand plateaus. Can you characterize the inference versus training split in Data Center today and whether inference capex sustains through fiscal 2026?

Colette Kress: Vivek, the inference versus training mix has shifted — today it's roughly 40 percent training and 60 percent inference. The inference load is growing rapidly as AI deployment scales to billions of users through ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and other consumer applications. We expect inference to represent 65 to 70 percent of Data Center by end of fiscal 2026. The key insight is that inference is not a one-time training spike — it's an ongoing compute demand that compounds with user growth. Each new enterprise AI deployment adds perpetual inference revenue. We see inference spending from hyperscalers growing 40 to 50 percent year over year through 2026. The training market is not slowing — it's growing but at a slower rate, because AI model training runs are running more frequently as companies compete in AI. The data center market for AI will exceed $500 billion by 2028.
sections.forward_outlook: Jensen Huang: We are at the very beginning of a new industrial revolution. The combination of language models, reasoning, and physical AI is going to transform every industry on the planet. We are building the infrastructure for the next decade. Every major technology company, every country, and every government will need AI infrastructure. Our competitive position has never been stronger — we are executing on the most complex supply chain in history, shipping products that are years ahead of competition, and building the world's largest AI developer ecosystem. We expect to grow for many years. The industrial adoption of AI is not a hype cycle — it is a structural shift that takes decades to play out. Thank you.
